where: Lead, second sentence and Section 1 opening
problem: The lead states flatly that every network application is a pair of processes in two places. Section 3 of the same chapter describes peer-to-peer applications where many processes take part and no fixed pair exists, so a student meets a claim the chapter itself later contradicts.
fix: Soften the framing: 'Most network applications you will meet are a pair of processes in two places: one asks for something, the other provides it.' Then Section 3 shows the peer-to-peer case where the roles sit on every machine.

problem: The sentence 'The client must not need to know the server's schedule' is unclear: it is not a property students will recognise, and it reads as if the client has to check some timetable. The intended point is simply that the server is always listening, so the client may knock at any time.
fix: Replace with: 'Because the server never sleeps, the client does not have to arrange a time to call; it can send its request whenever the user needs it.'
